props.title: Persona
props.initialSlug: Two women's identities merge in psychological duel

sections.content: **Persona** (1966) represents Ingmar Bergman's masterful dive into psychological horror and identity dissolution. The film follows a nurse (Bibi Andersson) caring for an actress (Liv Ullmann) who's gone mute, their identities gradually merging in a remote seaside cottage. Bergman's stark black-and-white cinematography and extreme close-ups created a template for art-house psychological thrillers like **Mulholland Drive** (2001) and **Black Swan** (2010). The film's famous face-merging sequence influenced everything from **Fight Club** (1999) to **Lost Highway** (1997).

sections.content: The film's influence on psychological horror cannot be overstated. **Perfect Blue** (1997) directly borrowed Persona's identity-melding narrative for its story of a pop idol and her stalker. **The Devil's Backbone** (2001) and **The Others** (2001) echo Persona's claustrophobic atmosphere and exploration of trauma through gothic horror elements. Robert Altman's **3 Women** (1977) is perhaps the most direct spiritual successor, following two women whose personalities begin to blur and swap. SUBHEAD: Identity and Performance in Cinema

Bergman's examination of performance and identity spawned countless imitators. **Mulholland Drive** (2001) uses similar doubling techniques to explore Hollywood's destructive nature. **Possession** (1981) takes the concept into body horror territory. Modern films like **The Double** (2013) and **Enemy** (2013) continue mining this territory of fractured identities and doppelgangers. Even mainstream thrillers like **Black Swan** (2010) owe a clear debt to Persona's groundbreaking exploration of psychological dissolution.
